hints: Start with what is already given as stage 1. Reduced NAD arrives from earlier respiration carrying hydrogen. Think about what must first be done to free usable protons and energetic electrons from it.
Follow the electrons once they are free. They do not jump straight to oxygen. Think about moving step by step through carriers and what is released at each small drop in energy level.
Link that released energy to movement of protons. Think about pumping from one side of the crista membrane to the other and what kind of gradient this builds up.
Finish the story by using the gradient. Think about diffusion back through a channel enzyme to make ATP, and what is left at the very end to combine protons, electrons and oxygen.
walkthrough:
Release the electrons from reduced NAD**
Reduced NAD from the Krebs cycle and link reaction is the starting donor. It releases hydrogen atoms to the first cytochrome carrier (V), then those hydrogen atoms split into protons and electrons (S). This gives free high-energy electrons to enter the chain and protons that will contribute to the gradient.

Pass electrons and pump protons to build the gradient**
Electrons are passed from carrier to carrier in a series of redox reactions (U). Energy released as electrons fall to lower energy levels is used to pump protons from the matrix into the intermembrane space (W). This sets up a proton electrochemical gradient across the crista membrane, high concentration outside and low inside (R).

Use the gradient to make ATP and remove electrons**
Protons diffuse back down their gradient through ATP synthase into the matrix (Q). The flow provides energy for ATP synthase to phosphorylate ADP to ATP (X). At the end of the chain, protons combine with electrons and oxygen to form water (T), which keeps electrons flowing by removing them.

hints: Picture a mitochondrion in section. There is a fluid-filled centre, a highly folded inner membrane, and a narrow intermembrane space. Every enzyme sits where its job needs it.
Sort the list into membrane jobs and fluid jobs. Anything that pumps protons or passes electrons needs to be embedded in a membrane that can hold a gradient.
Anything that is a soluble cycle of reactions in solution, using freely mixing substrates and enzymes, belongs in the large fluid compartment.
Remember ATP synthase is itself the proton channel. It must sit in exactly the same membrane across which the proton gradient was built.
Think about the journey of pyruvate. It enters from the cytoplasm after glycolysis and is then processed with coenzyme A to feed acetyl CoA into the Krebs cycle, all in the same fluid compartment.
walkthrough:
Membrane proteins live in the crista membrane**
The inner membrane is folded into cristae to give a huge surface area for electron carriers and ATP synthase. The electron transport chain carriers are embedded here so they can pump protons from matrix to intermembrane space. ATP synthase spans the same inner membrane so protons can flow back through it down the gradient.

Soluble pathways live in the matrix**
The matrix is the aqueous centre containing soluble enzymes, coenzymes and substrates. The Krebs cycle enzymes are here, so the Krebs cycle occurs in the matrix. Coenzyme A, which carries acetate as acetyl CoA into the cycle, is also in the matrix.

Link pyruvate entry to the matrix**
Pyruvate diffuses in from the cytoplasm after glycolysis. Pyruvate decarboxylation to acetyl CoA by pyruvate dehydrogenase occurs in the matrix, so pyruvate is located in the matrix to feed the link reaction and then the Krebs cycle.
Final answer: ATP synthase - inner membrane / cristae; Krebs cycle - matrix; electron transport chain - inner membrane / cristae; coenzyme A - matrix; pyruvate - matrix.
